title: Migrated queries run 60% faster — should we move everything?

scenario.role: You're the analytics engineer at Beacon
scenario.situation: Over the last quarter the platform team moved a slice of the warehouse workload from the old engine onto Nimbus, a new query engine. Raj, the Head of Data Platform, pulled the query logs and is delighted: queries running on Nimbus average about 12 seconds versus 33 seconds on the old engine — roughly 60% faster. He wants to migrate the entire remaining workload next quarter and quote the compute savings to Finance. He needs your read on the logs first.
scenario.stakeholderBelief: "Nimbus runs queries ~60% faster. Migrating everything else is a no-brainer — same queries, big speedup, lower bill."
scenario.question: Is the 60% speedup real? Estimate what Nimbus actually does to query runtime, and tell Raj what to expect if the rest of the workload moves over.

columns.name: team
columns.description: Owning team: growth, finance, product, platform, or ml

columns.name: query_type
columns.description: Workload class: dashboard, adhoc, etl, or ml_features

columns.name: bytes_scanned_gb
columns.description: Data scanned by the query, in GB — the dominant driver of how long a query takes

columns.name: table_count
columns.description: Number of tables joined in the query

columns.name: scheduled_hour
columns.description: Hour of day the query ran (0-23)

columns.name: migrated
columns.description: 1 if the query ran on the new Nimbus engine, else 0 (old engine)

columns.name: runtime_sec
columns.description: Wall-clock runtime in seconds — the outcome

guidingQuestions: Reproduce Raj's number: what's the average runtime on Nimbus (migrated = 1) versus the old engine (migrated = 0)?
Which queries actually got migrated? Compare bytes_scanned_gb for migrated vs non-migrated queries — were the two groups running the same kind of work?
bytes_scanned_gb is the main thing that makes a query slow. If it also predicts which queries were migrated, what does that do to the naive comparison?

Estimate the engine effect holding query size constant — bucket queries by bytes_scanned_gb (deciles) and compare migrated vs not within each bucket, or model log(runtime) ~ log(bytes) + migrated. How big is the speedup now?
What do you tell Raj to expect when the heavy ETL and ML queries — the ones still on the old engine — move to Nimbus?
suggestedApproach: Compute the headline first — mean runtime by migrated — so you know the exact claim you're testing.

Before crediting the engine, profile what was migrated: compare bytes_scanned_gb (and query_type) across the two groups. If they aren't running comparable work, the raw gap isn't an engine comparison.
Query size dwarfs almost everything else in runtime. If small queries were migrated first, size is confounding the comparison — account for it by stratifying on bytes or regressing on log(bytes).
Re-estimate the migrated effect within size buckets and check it's stable; a percentage (ratio) effect travels better across sizes than an absolute second count.
Translate the adjusted effect into a forecast for the un-migrated heavy workload, and note what a clean test would look like (run the same queries on both engines).

notebook.intro: Five steps: reproduce the speed-up, profile what was migrated, then compare engines on comparable queries.

cells.title: Reproduce the headline
cells.explain: Mean runtime by migrated — the claim behind moving everything.
cells.code:
means = df.groupby("migrated")["runtime_sec"].mean()
headline_ratio = means[1] / means[0]
print(f"migrated runs {1 - headline_ratio:.1%} faster on the raw comparison")
means.round(2)
cells.reads: The raw speed-up is dramatic. What was migrated matters before it can be credited to the engine.

cells.title: Profile what was migrated
cells.explain: Compare query size and type across the two groups. If the small queries moved first, this is not an engine comparison.
cells.code:
profile = df.groupby("migrated")[["bytes_scanned_gb", "table_count"]].mean()
profile["n"] = df.groupby("migrated").size()
print("what each engine is actually running:")
print(profile.round(2))
pd.crosstab(df["migrated"], df["query_type"], normalize="index").round(3) * 100
cells.reads: The migrated workload is far lighter. The old engine is carrying the heavy queries.

cells.title: Check size drives runtime
cells.explain: Query size dwarfs almost everything else in runtime. Bin bytes scanned and look.
cells.code:
df["size_band"] = pd.qcut(df["bytes_scanned_gb"], 5, labels=False, duplicates="drop")
by_band = df.groupby("size_band")["runtime_sec"].mean()
print("mean runtime by query-size band (seconds)")
by_band.round(2)
cells.reads: Runtime is driven overwhelmingly by bytes scanned — the variable that also decided migration order.

cells.title: Compare within size bands
cells.explain: Hold size constant. A ratio travels across sizes in a way an absolute second count does not, so compare ratios.
cells.code:
within = df.groupby(["size_band", "migrated"])["runtime_sec"].mean().unstack()
within["speed_up"] = 1 - within[1] / within[0]
print("within-band speed-up (fraction faster):")
within.round(3)
cells.reads: Inside each size band the speed-up is real but much smaller, and reasonably stable across bands.

cells.title: Forecast the heavy workload
cells.explain: Apply the like-for-like ratio rather than the headline to what has not moved yet.
cells.code:
weights = df["size_band"].value_counts(normalize=True)
adjusted = within[[0, 1]].mul(weights, axis=0).sum()
adj_speed_up = 1 - adjusted[1] / adjusted[0]
pd.DataFrame(
    {"speed-up": [1 - headline_ratio, adj_speed_up]},
    index=["raw comparison", "same query size"],
).round(3)
cells.reads: Promising the headline number for the un-migrated heavy queries would promise a speed-up that came from picking easy work first.

teachingNote.naiveRead: Queries on Nimbus average ~12.0s versus ~32.6s on the old engine — about a 63% reduction. Taken at face value, Nimbus looks like a massive, free speedup and migrating everything looks like pure savings.
teachingNote.theTrap: The workload was not migrated at random. The small, cheap queries went first: migrated queries scanned about 2.4 GB on average, versus 7.3 GB for the queries left on the old engine — roughly 3x smaller. Bytes scanned is the dominant driver of runtime, so the migrated group was fast *before* Nimbus ever touched it. Most of the 20-second gap is the size difference between the two groups, not the engine. Comparing a bag of light dashboard queries against a bag of heavy ETL scans measures the queries, not the warehouse.
teachingNote.honestAnswer: Hold query size constant — bucket queries into bytes-scanned deciles and compare migrated vs not within each bucket (or regress log(runtime) on log(bytes) + migrated) — and Nimbus's edge shrinks to about a 12% speedup. Real and worth having, but a fifth of the headline. When the heavy ETL/ML queries move over, expect ~12% off their runtime, not 60% — so budget the savings against that, not against the raw average.
howToGetThere: Compute the naive gap: mean(runtime_sec) for migrated=1 vs migrated=0 → ~12.0s vs ~32.6s (−63%). That's Raj's number.
Profile the treated group: mean(bytes_scanned_gb) by migrated → ~2.4 GB vs ~7.3 GB. The migrated queries are far smaller.
Recognise bytes_scanned_gb as a confounder: it drives runtime AND predicts migration, so it inflates the raw comparison.
Adjust — stratify on bytes deciles and take the size-weighted within-bucket runtime ratio, or fit log(runtime) ~ log(bytes) + table_count + migrated. The engine effect lands near −12%.
Sanity-check: the adjusted effect is far smaller than the naive one and roughly constant across size buckets — a genuine engine speedup, not a workload artifact.

numbers.label: Mean GB scanned — migrated vs not

teachingNote.lesson: A raw average that compares two groups doing different work is a comparison of the work, not the treatment. Nimbus was handed the easy queries, so it looked three times better than it is. Before attributing a performance win to a new tool, ask what it was run on — and match like with like. The transferable move is to adjust for the dominant driver (here, bytes scanned) and express the effect as a percentage that holds across sizes. The only clean way to know is to run the same queries on both engines; short of that, forecast the migration savings against the ~12% adjusted effect, not the 60% mirage.
